content.title: Compound interest
content.prompt: What do you already know about compound interest? Explain it as if to a smart friend who has never invested.

learning.short: Compound interest is interest earned on both the original principal and on previously accumulated interest, so growth accelerates over time.
learning.detailed:
With simple interest you earn a fixed amount each period on the original sum. With compound interest each period's earnings are added to the balance, and the next period's interest is calculated on the larger amount. Over short horizons the difference is small; over decades it dominates. A useful shortcut is the rule of 72: divide 72 by the annual rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double. At 7 percent that is roughly ten years.

The same mechanism works against you with debt. Credit-card balances compound at high rates, which is why small balances become large ones. It also applies beyond money: skills, audiences and codebases compound when each gain makes the next gain easier.
key_points: Growth on growth: interest is reinvested and itself earns interest.
Time matters more than rate at the start; rate matters more later.
Rule of 72 estimates doubling time.
Fees and inflation compound negatively.
Starting early beats contributing more later.
examples: 1,000 at 7 percent for 40 years becomes about 15,000; for 20 years only about 3,900.
A 1 percent annual fund fee can consume roughly a quarter of returns over 30 years.
common_mistakes: Confusing annual percentage rate with effective annual rate.
Underestimating how long the flat early part of the curve lasts.
Ignoring that inflation compounds too.

content.title: Cognitive biases
content.prompt: Name and explain three cognitive biases that affect engineering decisions.

learning.short: Cognitive biases are systematic deviations from rational judgment. In engineering they show up as sunk-cost thinking, overconfidence in estimates and anchoring on the first design proposed.
learning.detailed:
Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky documented dozens of biases that arise from fast, intuitive thinking. Three matter constantly in software work. The sunk-cost fallacy keeps teams investing in a failing rewrite because so much has already been spent. The planning fallacy makes estimates optimistic even when the estimator knows previous estimates were wrong. Anchoring means the first number or design mentioned in a meeting shapes everything that follows.

The defense is process, not willpower. Pre-mortems, reference-class forecasting (comparing to similar past projects) and blind estimation before discussion reduce the effect. Naming the bias in the room helps only when the culture tolerates it.
key_points: Biases are systematic, not random, so they can be designed around.
Sunk cost: past investment should not influence future decisions.
Planning fallacy: use outside-view data from comparable projects.
Anchoring: collect independent opinions before discussing.
Confirmation bias: seek disconfirming evidence deliberately.
examples: A team continues a two-year migration because 'we have come this far'.
Estimates cluster around whatever number the senior engineer says first.
common_mistakes: Believing awareness alone removes the bias.
Using 'bias' as a rhetorical weapon rather than a diagnostic.

content.title: Supply and demand
content.prompt: Explain supply and demand, and use it to explain why senior engineer salaries rose so fast in the 2010s.

learning.short: Prices move toward the point where the quantity people want to buy equals the quantity sellers want to sell. When demand rises faster than supply, prices rise.
learning.detailed:
The supply curve shows how much sellers will offer at each price; the demand curve shows how much buyers will take. Their intersection is the equilibrium. Shifts, not movements along the curves, explain most real-world price changes: new demand (every company becoming a software company) shifts demand right, while supply of experienced engineers is slow to grow because experience takes years. Result: wages rise until the gap closes, either by more people entering, by substitution (tools, offshoring, AI), or by demand falling.

Elasticity describes how responsive quantity is to price. Senior engineering talent is inelastic in the short run, which is why salaries spiked rather than merely rising.
key_points: Equilibrium is where supply meets demand.
Shifts of a curve cause price changes; movements along a curve are responses.
Short-run supply of skilled labour is inelastic.
Substitutes (AI, offshoring) shift demand for a given input.
Prices are information about scarcity.
examples: 2021 hiring boom: demand shift right, wages spike; 2023 layoffs: demand shift left.
GPU prices during AI training booms.
common_mistakes: Confusing a shift with a movement along the curve.
Treating price as unfair rather than as a signal.

content.title: The scientific method
content.prompt: Describe the scientific method and explain how you would apply it to debugging a production incident.

learning.short: Observe, form a falsifiable hypothesis, design a test that could prove it wrong, run it, update your belief. Debugging is this loop with a shorter cycle.
learning.detailed:
The core idea, sharpened by Karl Popper, is falsifiability: a good hypothesis makes a prediction that could fail. Debugging goes wrong when engineers change several things at once (no controlled variable), when they look for confirming evidence ('the logs are consistent with my theory') instead of disconfirming evidence, and when they skip forming a hypothesis at all and just try things.

A disciplined incident investigation states the hypothesis out loud ('the cache is returning stale user records'), identifies the observation that would refute it ('if I bypass the cache, the bug persists'), runs that check, and records the result. This keeps the team from re-testing the same theories and produces a post-mortem timeline almost for free.
key_points: Hypotheses must be falsifiable.
Change one variable at a time.
Look for evidence that would prove you wrong.
Record what was tested and the result.
Reproduce before you fix.
examples: Bisecting a regression across commits is a controlled experiment.
A/B tests are the scientific method applied to product decisions.
common_mistakes: Fixing symptoms whose cause was never confirmed.
Confusing correlation in a dashboard with cause.

content.title: The printing press
content.prompt: What did the printing press change, and what is the closest modern parallel?

learning.short: Gutenberg's movable-type press (around 1450) cut the cost of copying text by orders of magnitude, which broke the church's and scribes' monopoly on information and fuelled the Reformation, science and literacy.
learning.detailed:
Before the press, a book took months to copy by hand and cost roughly a year's wages. Within fifty years of Gutenberg, Europe had printed some twenty million volumes. Cheap copying did several things at once: it standardized texts (errors stopped accumulating), created a market for vernacular writing, and let ideas spread faster than authorities could suppress them. Luther's theses spread across Germany in weeks. Scientific results could be compared across cities because everyone had the same edition.

The usual modern parallel is the internet, and the analogy holds for the collapse of distribution cost and the loss of gatekeepers. It also holds for the side effects: a century of pamphlet wars, misinformation and religious conflict followed the press before institutions adapted.
key_points: Cost of copying fell by roughly a thousand-fold.
Standardization enabled cumulative science.
Gatekeepers lost control of information.
Disruption took decades to stabilize.
Literacy and the market for ideas grew together.
examples: Luther's Ninety-five Theses reprinted across Europe within months.
Vesalius's anatomy with identical woodcuts in every copy.
common_mistakes: Treating Gutenberg as sole inventor; movable type existed in Korea and China earlier.
Assuming information technology only has positive effects.

content.title: Stoicism
content.prompt: What is Stoicism, and what is one Stoic idea you could apply to leading a team?

learning.short: Stoicism is a Greek and Roman philosophy that teaches focusing on what is within your control (your judgments and actions), accepting what is not, and acting with virtue regardless of outcome.
learning.detailed:
Founded by Zeno around 300 BC and developed by Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius, Stoicism holds that suffering comes from judgments about events rather than events themselves. The 'dichotomy of control' separates what depends on us (opinions, intentions, effort) from what does not (reputation, outcomes, other people). Virtue, meaning wisdom, courage, justice and temperance, is the only true good.

For leaders this translates into practical habits: prepare for setbacks in advance (premeditatio malorum), respond to incidents with the calm that the team will copy, and judge yourself on process rather than on quarterly results you cannot fully control. Critics note that Stoicism can slide into passivity or emotional suppression if misread; the original texts stress action and duty.
key_points: Dichotomy of control.
Judgments, not events, cause distress.
Virtue as the only unconditional good.
Negative visualization to reduce fear and increase gratitude.
Act for the common good; you are part of a whole.
examples: A CTO who separates 'we shipped a bad release' (in control: process) from 'the customer left' (not fully in control).
Marcus Aurelius writing Meditations as a private journal while running an empire at war.
common_mistakes: Confusing Stoicism with being unemotional.
Using 'not in my control' to avoid responsibility.

content.title: Inflation
content.prompt: Explain what inflation is, what causes it, and why central banks raise interest rates to fight it.

learning.short: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, meaning each unit of money buys less. It is driven by demand outrunning supply, by rising input costs, or by expectations that prices will keep rising.
learning.detailed:
Economists distinguish demand-pull inflation (too much money chasing too few goods, as after large stimulus), cost-push inflation (energy shocks, supply-chain breaks) and built-in inflation (workers and firms raising wages and prices because they expect inflation). Central banks target around 2 percent because mild inflation greases wage adjustments and avoids deflation, which makes debt heavier and delays spending.

Raising the policy interest rate makes borrowing more expensive, which cools investment, housing and consumer credit, lowering demand. It works with a lag of a year or more, which is why central banks are often accused of acting too late or too hard. Rate rises do little against supply-side inflation except by reducing demand until it matches the reduced supply.
key_points: Measured by a price index such as CPI.
Three causes: demand-pull, cost-push, expectations.
Central banks target roughly 2 percent.
Rates act through credit and demand with long lags.
Deflation is also harmful.
examples: 2021–2023 inflation: stimulus plus supply chains plus energy.
1970s stagflation: oil shock with entrenched expectations.
common_mistakes: Thinking inflation means prices of everything rise equally.
Assuming printing money is the only cause.

content.title: Product-market fit
content.prompt: What is product-market fit, how do you know you have it, and what do founders get wrong about it?

learning.short: Product-market fit is the point where a product satisfies strong demand from a well-defined market: customers pull it from you, retention is strong, and growth stops requiring force.
learning.detailed:
Marc Andreessen popularized the term: you can always feel when it is not happening (sales cycles drag, users churn, press is lukewarm) and when it is (servers fall over, hiring cannot keep up). Quantitatively, teams look at retention curves that flatten rather than decay to zero, at the Sean Ellis test (over 40 percent of users would be 'very disappointed' without the product), and at organic growth share.

Founders commonly mistake early enthusiasm for fit, confuse a market that exists with a market that will pay, and reach fit in a niche then break it by expanding too fast. Fit is also not permanent; markets move and competitors copy.
key_points: Demand pulls the product; you are not pushing it.
Retention curve flattens.
Sean Ellis 40 percent test.
Fit is per segment, not global.
It can be lost.
examples: Slack's early growth came from teams inviting teams without a sales force.
Many 2021 startups had 'funding-market fit' rather than product-market fit.
common_mistakes: Scaling sales and marketing before fit.
Measuring signups instead of retention.

content.title: Deep work
content.prompt: What is deep work, why is it hard, and how would you design an engineering team's week around it?

learning.short: Deep work, a term from Cal Newport, is focused, distraction-free effort on cognitively demanding tasks. It produces most of the value in knowledge work but is constantly displaced by shallow tasks.
learning.detailed:
Attention residue means that after a context switch, part of your attention stays on the previous task for some time, so fragmented days produce shallow output even when hours are long. Newport argues deep work is both increasingly valuable and increasingly rare, hence a competitive advantage.

For teams, the practical levers are: protecting large blocks (no-meeting mornings or days), batching communication, making written asynchronous updates the default, and reducing the number of channels that expect immediate response. Managers should measure output rather than responsiveness. The failure mode is treating deep work as an individual discipline problem when the environment makes it impossible.
key_points: Context switching leaves attention residue.
Value comes from focused blocks, not total hours.
Protect blocks at the team level.
Make async the default; sync the exception.
Measure output, not availability.
examples: A team that moved standup to written form and added Tuesday and Thursday no-meeting days.
Maker's schedule versus manager's schedule.
common_mistakes: Blaming individuals for a calendar the organization created.
Confusing being busy with being productive.

content.title: Game theory basics
content.prompt: Explain the prisoner's dilemma and give one example of it in a software company.

learning.short: The prisoner's dilemma shows how two rational parties can each choose to defect even though cooperating would leave both better off, because defecting is individually safer whatever the other does.
learning.detailed:
Two suspects are questioned separately. Each can stay silent or betray. Betrayal is the dominant strategy for each, yet mutual betrayal is worse for both than mutual silence. The dilemma dissolves when the game repeats: in iterated play, strategies like tit-for-tat (cooperate first, then mirror) sustain cooperation because defection is punished next round.

In companies the pattern appears whenever short-term individual incentives conflict with shared outcomes: teams skipping tests to hit their own deadline while relying on others to keep the build green, or departments hoarding headcount. The remedies are the same as in theory: make the game repeated, make behaviour visible, and align incentives with the shared payoff.
key_points: Dominant strategy can lead to a worse collective outcome.
Repetition and reputation enable cooperation.
Tit-for-tat is simple and robust.
Transparency changes the payoff matrix.
Nash equilibrium is not the same as the best outcome.
examples: Two teams sharing an on-call rotation, each tempted to ship risky changes on Friday.
Price wars between competitors.
common_mistakes: Assuming people are irrational when incentives explain the behaviour.
Forgetting that most real games are repeated.

content.title: Positioning
content.prompt: What is positioning in marketing, and how would you position a developer tool?

learning.short: Positioning is the deliberate choice of which market category your product belongs to, who it is for, and what alternative it beats, so that customers can quickly understand and value it.
learning.detailed:
April Dunford's framework starts from the competitive alternatives (what customers would do without you), your unique attributes, the value those attributes enable, the customers who care most about that value, and finally the market category that makes the value obvious. Good positioning is a choice; weak positioning tries to serve everyone.

For a developer tool the alternatives are usually 'do it by hand' or 'a script we wrote', not a competitor. The customers who care most are the ones whose pain is frequent and expensive. Category choice matters: 'observability platform' sets expectations and comparisons very different from 'error tracker'.
key_points: Start from competitive alternatives, not features.
Pick the best-fit customer, not the widest.
Category frames the comparison.
Positioning is a decision, then messaging.
Revisit as the market moves.
examples: Slack: 'email replacement' vs 'chat app'.
Postgres hosts positioning as 'serverless Postgres' vs 'managed database'.
common_mistakes: Listing features instead of the alternative you beat.
Positioning against a competitor customers have never heard of.

content.title: Semiconductor geopolitics
content.prompt: Why are advanced semiconductors at the centre of geopolitics, and what is Taiwan's role?

learning.short: Cutting-edge chips power AI, weapons and every modern industry, yet their manufacturing is concentrated in a few firms, chiefly TSMC in Taiwan, making the supply chain both a strategic asset and a vulnerability.
learning.detailed:
Leading-edge fabrication requires extreme-ultraviolet lithography machines (made only by ASML in the Netherlands), years of process know-how and tens of billions of dollars per fab. TSMC produces the large majority of the most advanced logic chips, including those designed by Nvidia and Apple. This concentration means a conflict over Taiwan would disrupt global technology production within weeks.

The United States has responded with export controls on advanced chips and equipment to China and with subsidies (the CHIPS Act) to rebuild domestic fabrication; China is investing heavily in self-sufficiency; Europe, Japan and Korea are courting fabs. For technologists the implications include hardware lead times, AI compute access and the strategic value of software that runs on less-advanced hardware.
key_points: Extreme concentration: TSMC, Samsung, Intel at the leading edge; ASML alone for EUV.
Chips are dual-use: consumer and military.
Export controls have become a primary policy tool.
Reshoring fabs is slow and expensive.
Taiwan's 'silicon shield' argument.
examples: 2022 US export controls on advanced GPUs to China.
Automotive production halts during the 2021 chip shortage.
common_mistakes: Assuming a new fab can replace TSMC in a few years.
Conflating chip design (fabless) with manufacturing.
